TOKYO, Nov 19 : Japanese gas utility Osaka Gas will continue expanding its businesses in the US and India despite rising global geopolitical risks, President Masataka Fujiwara said on Thursday. • Osaka Gas produces and sells US shale gas to domestic customers, and is expanding sales of domestically produced natural gas and renewable energy development in India • The company is not concerned about securing liquefied natural gas supplies for the peak winter demand season as it has no contracts requiring shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and has secured most supplies under long-term contracts, Executive Officer Sunao Okamoto said • However, lower-than-usual European gas inventories could lead to competition between Europe and Asia for spot LNG after the winter, potentially pushing up prices, Okamoto said

• Osaka Gas decided to exit the Greater Sunrise gas project, whose gas fields lie between East Timor and Australia, after participating since 2000, as development had made little progress and it was time to move on as part of a portfolio reshuffle, Okamoto said • In September, Osaka Gas bought a 5 per cent stake in Australia's Browse gas project. Okamoto said the company expects the project to eventually move forward and values Australia as a Japanese ally with no major shipping chokepoints. The project would also allow Osaka Gas to secure LNG on a free-on-board basis from its own equity production • Osaka Gas has long-term LNG contracts with Australia, the US, Papua New Guinea and Russia, after contracts with Malaysia, Brunei and Oman expired in recent years. Its LNG transaction volume reached 12.4 million metric tons in the financial year that ended March 2026, with 20 per cent coming from its equity investments in upstream gas projects

FAST

SEOUL: South Korea's exports so far for this year have exceeded US$1 trillion, driven by a global AI chip boom, making it the fourth country in the world to reach the milestone after Germany, the United States and China. Exports passed the US$1 trillion mark on Thursday (Nov 19), compared with last year's record of US$709 billion, the trade ministry said. The export surge has been led by the semiconductor sector as AI investment drives demand , while other traditional manufacturing sectors, such as autos, steel and ships, have lagged amid global protectionism triggered by US tariffs and geopolitical conflicts such as the Iran war. In the first three quarters of 2026, semiconductor exports jumped 184 per cent from a year earlier to account for 42 per cent of the country's total exports, more than double their average 20 per cent share over the past five years.

"Now, we need to turn this achievement into sustainable growth. We will enhance the competitiveness of major industries and grow future growth engines, such as AI and bio," President Lee Jae Myung said in a social media post on X. "Most of all, the achievement in exports should improve the lives of the people. We will create 'growth for all', sharing the opportunities and fruits of growth with big and small companies as well as the capital area and regional areas," Lee said. Despite record exports, domestic demand in Asia's fourth-largest economy remains weak, with the benefits of the export boom yet to trickle down to many households. Consumer sentiment has been hurt by high interest rates and prices, as well as unprecedented volatility in the domestic stock market. As part of efforts to tackle widening inequality in a two-speed economy, the Lee administration plans to create a 162.3 trillion won (US$121.94 billion) Future Response Fund to funnel excess tax revenue from the chip boom toward growth industries, young people, regional development and education. "The government and the private sector will have to work together to strengthen the cycle of exports leading to domestic investment and job creation, as well as the revitalisation of regional economies, so that all people share the benefits of export growth in their daily lives," the country's six major business groups said in a joint statement, welcoming the US$1 trillion milestone. Economic growth in South Korea, home to leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, is expected to accelerate to the mid-3 per cent range this year, after expanding 1 per cent last year, as the AI boom fuels exports and investments , the finance minister said last month.

TOKYO: The global launch of Grand Theft Auto VI on Thursday (Nov 19) is expected to provide a major boost to PlayStation maker Sony - albeit not in its home market of Japan, where the franchise is a niche pursuit. The long-awaited open-world crime action game from Take-Two Interactive's Rockstar Games is rolling out across the world and has been met with rave reviews and fans taking time off work to play. Three-quarters of the 17 million GTA VI units sold are on PlayStation, according to estimates from Sensor Tower, outselling Xbox maker Microsoft. Shares in Sony, whose PlayStation 5 console is in its seventh year on the market, were up 2.8 per cent in Tokyo compared with flat trading in the benchmark index.

Analysts think that momentum is unlikely to extend to Japan, where Switch 2 maker Nintendo dominates the gaming device market and consumers prefer anime-style titles to realistic, violent Western games. "The current trends in Japan don't really fit this kind of game," said Toyo Securities analyst Hideki Yasuda. "It won't sell much in Japan, but there's absolutely no need for this game to sell in Japan," he said. Earlier this year Sony scored a major global success with movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day but in Japan faced competition from breakout hit Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of Mermaid Island. " A few of my friends bought GTA VI at midnight but I'm in no hurry to as it's only on PS5 and Xbox and you can't play multiplayer online yet," said Sorataka Goto, 33, who was shopping in Tokyo's Akihabara electronics district. "If and when it's on PC and you can play online I'll consider buying it," said Goto, who bought the remake of the The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Nintendo has sold more than five million copies of the Switch 2 title, which was originally on the Nintendo 64, in the first four days since its launch earlier this month. "I had the original as a child and so was excited to try this version," he said. SONY FACING PROCUREMENT HEADWINDS Analysts expect the release of GTA VI to soften the decline of PS5 hardware sales this year and support growth in software sales. Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 units during the July to September quarter, which analysts see as reflecting demand ahead of GTA VI, down from 4 million a year earlier. "We've modeled PlayStation profits materially ahead of the Street in the next couple of quarters, on account of the 'GTA VI' launch," Bernstein analyst David Dai wrote in a note. The release is bolstering Sony's games slate after it delayed the launch of God of War Laufey by three months to May 2027. Sony is grappling with procurement challenges as the cost of memory chips has risen sharply due to the AI boom. "I don't get the sense that Sony has much desire to aggressively sell hardware ... the benefits Sony gets from royalties will be enormous," said Toyo Securities' Yasuda.

Source: Reuters/lk

Nov 19 : Challenger rebuffed an improved takeover proposal from a unit of Japan's Daiichi Life that valued the Australian investment manager at A$8.17 billion ($5.48 billion), sending its shares to a four-week low on Thursday. Daiichi Life's revised offer for the remaining 79.5 per cent of Challenger shares it does not already own was A$12.20 apiece, a 2.1 per cent premium to the stock's last close and 40 Australian cents above its previous offer. Challenger's board said the revised offer from the Japanese insurer does not "adequately represent fair value" for shareholders in the context of a control transaction. Daiichi Life did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Challenger's shares slid as much as 2.7 per cent to A$11.63 in early Sydney trade, their lowest level since October 22. They were last down 2.1 per cent as of 0228 GMT, compared with a 0.8 per cent decline in the broader market. "The Challenger board, in our view, would be open to a deal, but the premium would clearly need to be higher to start the deal process formally," said Cameron Curko, CIO at Pitcher Partners Sydney. The strength of their underlying business of late gives them a "strong hand" to demand more, he added. TAL Daiichi Life Australia Pty currently owns 20.47 per cent of Challenger, LSEG data showed. Japan's appetite for Australian dealmaking is hardly new. ORIX Corp and a Sumitomo Corp-led consortium were among those vying for vehicle leasing company FleetPartners. Local media reported last month that Suncorp and suitor Tokio Marine had engaged in preliminary takeover discussions, a report the Australian insurer subsequently denied. CHICAGO, Nov 18 : The state of Arizona has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies relating to the "apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents," Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said Wednesday. A criminal investigation does not necessarily mean charges will be brought. Mayes said her office was investigating whether Arizona state law was being violated on an ongoing basis.  "The state of Arizona is very worried about this, and we are looking at it from multiple angles," Mayes told a press conference in Chicago. Mayes declined to identify the other companies her office was investigating. She said her office had been in contact with Arizona banks, but declined to name them or give their responses.

A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The banking industry has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth. Reuters reported last month that major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions.  Mayes' comments come two days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI for allegedly developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had carried out cyberattacks independently. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on that lawsuit, but the company has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior and said it was reinforcing its safeguards. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain.”

WASHINGTON, Nov 18 : A federal grand jury has indicted a Russian national on charges of acting as a foreign agent to target the technology and defense company Palantir and surveil its employees, according to court documents and two people familiar with the matter. Working with Russian collaborators, Igor D'iu allegedly traveled from Russia and stalked employees of what the Justice Department described in its affidavit and press release only as a Silicon Valley technology and defense company. Two people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, identified the company as Palantir Technologies Inc, which has a large office in Palo Alto, California but is based in Florida.  D'iu took photos of employees' computer screens while at a coffee shop near company offices, according to the affidavit. He also followed a female staff member nearly 30 miles (50 km)  but stopped his pursuit after the employee contacted the police, prosecutors said.

“The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company’s assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia,” Craig H. Missakian, the top federal prosecutor in San Francisco, said in a statement. Palantir CEO Alex Karp has publicly backed Ukraine, and the company has said it deployed its technology to the country. Palantir did not respond to a request for comment. Russia's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. One of the people, who is familiar with the company's thinking, said the attempted breach was unsuccessful and will not change the company's support for Ukraine. The person added that Palantir is unlikely to be the only technology and defense company targeted by the Russians. News of the alleged surveillance comes amid heightened scrutiny of tech company security after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in the wake of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of having Chinese intelligence ties. D'iu, who is being held in federal custody, is charged with two counts related to his alleged work as a Russian agent, one count of interstate stalking and one count of fraud related to identification documents. He faces up to 21 years in prison. Reuters could not immediately determine if he had appointed a lawyer.  Bloomberg first reported that Palantir was the target of the Russian surveillance campaign.  D'iu allegedly entered the United States through the Texas-Mexico border in July and searched for company employee addresses online in August, according to the indictment. After following two employees on consecutive days out of the company's Palo Alto offices in early September, he was contacted by local law enforcement. FBI agents later found a falsified US passport, Russian passports, roughly $18,000 in cash and 10 handwritten addresses, at least five of which were linked with employees' home addresses. Prosecutors said his co-conspirators told him he was working for "the Motherland" and directed him to set up his computer near the tech company's offices so they could try to obtain information from nearby employees.  He is next scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday.

Source: Reuters

A United States House panel asked Microsoft on Wednesday (Nov 18) to brief lawmakers on a report which said the company could allow the Chinese firm ByteDance to use OpenAI models through Microsoft's Azure cloud platform. Technology news outlet The Information reported that Microsoft was nearing a US$500 million deal with ByteDance. The chairman of the House Select Committee on China, John Moolenaar, said the panel wanted more details "given serious concerns over American companies helping China catch up to the US in the AI race". "Microsoft takes misuse of its AI services seriously and is committed to enforcing its terms of service, complying with applicable laws, and honouring its partner agreements," a Microsoft spokesperson said, adding that the company does not comment on confidential customer negotiations.

Washington has stressed the need for the US to be ahead of China in the AI race. In recent weeks, media reports about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy have increased scrutiny on technology business ties. Moolenaar, a Michigan Republican, said it was unacceptable for Microsoft, as a Pentagon contractor, to sell AI services to ByteDance.  "Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance," Moolenaar said in a statement.  "Leading American technology companies should not be playing both sides of the US-China AI race." Microsoft is also pursuing deals to sell OpenAI models to other Chinese businesses, including Alibaba, according to the Information report.  OpenAI prevents most Chinese firms from using its AI, but Microsoft has the rights to sell OpenAI's technology and does not impose the same restrictions, the Information said.

item.description: Anthropic said the IPO was priced at US$83 apiece, above its previously targeted range and valuing the company at approximately US$1.5 trillion.

Anthropic clinches biggest IPO ever with US$81 billion offering

Anthropic said the IPO was priced at US$83 apiece, above its previously targeted range and valuing the company at approximately US$1.5 trillion.

Anthropic's IPO raised US$81.31 billion on Wednesday (Nov 18), eclipsing SpaceX’s offering to claim the title of the largest stock-market debut on record. Anthropic said the IPO was priced at US$83 apiece, above its previously targeted range and valuing the company at approximately US$1.5 trillion. Reuters was first to report that the IPO was upsized by about 19 per cent to 980 million shares from its initial plan to sell 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 apiece.  Anthropic is also raising US$26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price, the filings show.

On a fully diluted basis, the IPO values the company at about US$1.5 trillion, including securities such as stock options and restricted stock. On a non-diluted basis, the valuation stands at about US$1.1 trillion. Anthropic, the first major frontier artificial-intelligence model developer to do an IPO, follows SpaceX's June offering, as investors jump at the chance for exposure to the fast-growing industry, even as the industry also faces mounting questions over the cost of developing and operating AI models.

Also read:

Commentary: Anthropic’s mega IPO is coming. Don’t let hype drive your investment decisions

CNA Explains: Why AI leaders are calling for a slowdown – and what makes it so difficult

CHALLENGING BACKDROP FOR AI STOCKS The AI lab comes to the public market just months after SpaceX's record-setting IPO, even as the backdrop for AI stocks has turned more challenging.  Chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure in recent weeks due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs and the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, a key pillar of the industry's growth. The pricing follows a roadshow that attracted demand several times the number of shares offered, Reuters previously reported, despite questions about the company's outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as competition in the AI industry intensifies. The company's closest rival, OpenAI, is also expected to pursue a public listing as early as next year. Anthropic's growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code, its coding agent that has gained popularity among software developers.  Its annualised revenue run rate reached US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from Sep 30, according to its IPO filing. The Claude maker said it had 11,900 customers generating at least US$100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of Sep 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of last year, underscoring its growing business foothold.

Also read:

Commentary: Anthropic’s call for AI development pause deserves attention. It also raises questions

Commentary: Some Anthropic engineers think AI might end us. Why race ahead?

SPENDING COMMITMENTS EXPOSE RISKS But sustaining that growth is becoming expensive. Anthropic spent nearly US$9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount spent a year earlier.  It also incurred an additional US$5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter, weighing on efficiency and reducing the revenue generated per dollar of computing capacity. Revenue rose 47 per cent in the third quarter to US$16.96 billion from the second quarter.  The company reported an operating loss of US$567 million, compared with operating income of US$974 million in the previous quarter.  The net loss narrowed to US$23.3 billion from US$66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating items related to bonds convertible into its shares. Anthropic has committed to nearly US$900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, part of its ongoing expenditures to train and operate increasingly powerful AI models. Its spending commitments also expose the company to risks beyond its own finances. Anthropic warned in its prospectus that some of its computing providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity. "If such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered," Anthropic said in an IPO filing. Investors have grown increasingly concerned about debt-fueled expansion of AI infrastructure, with technology companies and data-centre operators borrowing heavily to finance chips, power and computing facilities. Anthropic also faces questions over how it will balance its commercial ambitions with its emphasis on AI safety.  CEO Dario Amodei has called for the industry to slow the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models, warning that advances in AI could outstrip society's ability to manage the risks.

Also read:

Singapore backs international call for greater frontier AI safeguards

Existing safeguards by AI companies insufficient as models grow more capable: Josephine Teo

COMPETITION AND SAFETY CHALLENGES Competition is intensifying against Anthropic to be the leading provider of AI tools for businesses. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, its latest flagship AI model, accounted for about 13 per cent of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about 8 per cent for Anthropic's Claude Fable, according to data cited by Reuters in September.  OpenAI's annualised revenue run rate also passed US$40 billion in July, although Anthropic maintained a lead at the time. The competitive threat extends beyond the handful of companies developing the most powerful commercial models. More large companies are looking to adopt these models, which can be downloaded and run independently, to rein in AI spending. A recent Capgemini study found that 59 per cent of executives at large companies plan to increase their use of open-weight models over the next year as AI costs exceed budgets. Meta Platforms, one of Anthropic's largest customers, has been looking to reduce its use of the startup's models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, Reuters previously reported. "There's going to be other models out there ... Our thesis is that the vast amount of value will accrue to whoever is at the frontier," said Peter Singlehurst, head of private companies at Baillie Gifford, which invested roughly US$1.5 billion in Anthropic before its IPO.  "Our bet is that Anthropic has the ingredients - that doesn't guarantee, but means that they arguably have the highest probability of remaining at the frontier." Anthropic's IPO prospectus warned that its models could develop capabilities faster than the company could evaluate them and put adequate safeguards in place. "Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm," Anthropic said in the filing. The company has said it is considering tighter human oversight of some research and development decisions as its AI models take on a growing share of that work. Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters for Anthropic's offering, which has a 22-bank underwriting syndicate.  The two banks also served as lead underwriters for SpaceX's IPO earlier this year.

Source: Reuters/rl

Nov 18 : Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks raised its annual revenue forecast and signed a deal to acquire AI startup Applied Compute in a deal valued at $4.5 billion, as a heightened threat environment pushes customers toward broader security products. Shares of Palo Alto jumped about 10 per cent in after-hours trading to $368.60, and drove gains in rivals. CrowdStrike rose 5.3 per cent, Zscaler climbed 3 per cent and Fortinet gained 2.1 per cent. Palo Alto Networks has been repositioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, with recent deals, including its $3.35 billion acquisition of cloud management and monitoring firm Chronosphere and an agreement with Israeli startup Koi. The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks, giving attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities.

With the acquisition of Applied Compute, Palo Alto is looking to offer users a technology platform to help customers securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI. Open-weight models, AI systems whose trained settings are publicly released, present security challenges, including the risk of model tampering, data leakage and misuse by bad actors. "Applied Compute extends Palo Alto's push beyond traditional cybersecurity into enterprise AI. The opportunity is to bring AI infrastructure and security closer together," said Shaul Eyal, analyst at TD Cowen. The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027. Palo Alto now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion, compared with its prior expectation of $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion. FAST

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Anthropic's initial public offering is poised to create thousands of paper millionaires among current and former employees, in what could rank among the largest employee wealth windfalls in Silicon Valley history.   The offering is expected to unleash a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff who received stock grants as the Claude maker raced from startup to one of the world's most valuable companies. The IPO filing shows the amount of wealth embedded in employee stock awards, but not how that wealth is distributed among workers. As a result, outside estimates vary widely. Hill, a San Francisco marketplace for private-company shares, estimates 598 non-founder employees will hold at least $100 million in equity after the initial public offering, which is slated to open on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $83 a share, above its initial target range that would value the company at up to $1.4 trillion, according to a person familiar with the information.

Private-markets research firm Sacra estimates that roughly 2,800 current and former Anthropic employees could hold at least $1 million of pretax vested equity at a $1.35 trillion valuation, the middle of the price range.  The firms say their estimates are model-based and use public information. Reuters could not independently verify the estimates, which reflect factors including vesting periods, exercises, tender transactions, option awards, restricted stock units, award timing, headcount and employee retention rates. The filing does not disclose sums due individuals. But the wealth potentially shared by employees is vast.  Anthropic option holders were sitting on $119 billion of paper gains as of September 30, at a weighted average exercise price of $2.91 per share, the company disclosed. About $73 billion of that amount had vested through service and could be exercised immediately.  Anthropic did not respond to a comment request on the estimates. "The idea of equity appreciating to an amount that is life-changing is something that people strive for," Hill CEO Andrew Benson said. "It doesn't get better than this." EQUITY AT ENTRY LEVEL Workers who joined the firm when it started five years ago —  even in administrative positions and entry-level jobs — could be sitting on life-changing wealth, reflecting their holdings of stock options that carry exercise prices of less than $1.  Options granted through 2023 and still outstanding at the end of that year carried an average exercise price of 52 cents, the filing shows.  At SpaceX, which was founded in 2002 and went  public in June in a record-busting IPO, many of the employees who became millionaires had worked there for more than a decade.    "Early employees who started in a very junior role should have actually a better financial outcome than somebody who joined in a very senior role right before the IPO," Benson said, referring to Anthropic. Non-founder Anthropic employees can sell up to 10 per cent of their holdings on the first trading day, and up to another 35 per cent after fiscal 2026 earnings. EARLY HIRES REAP REWARDS Founded in 2021, the Claude maker expanded its workforce rapidly alongside the AI boom, growing to about 5,300 employees as of September 30 from roughly 940 at the end of 2024. As it hired aggressively, the company used stock-based compensation as a key recruiting tool. A May 2024 job posting for an administrative business partner role shows how the benefits of Anthropic's stock awards extended beyond AI researchers and engineers.  The position, which involved scheduling and managing calendars for company leaders, coordinating conference logistics and handling expense claims and reimbursements, paid an annual salary of $140,000 to $190,000.  The posting added that equity would be "a major component of the total compensation" beyond the salary, indicating that administrative and support staff were also eligible for stock awards alongside cash pay. That year, Anthropic said it granted employees options at an average exercise price of $1.30 per share. "And as we know from several anecdotes after the SpaceX IPO, this is often enough to help people down the organization chart do quite well in IPO," said Marcelo Ballve, head of research at Sacra. Anthropic granted CFO Krishna Rao 14 million stock options in 2024, also with a $1.30 exercise price, according to the filing. At the IPO price range, those options would carry roughly $1 billion in gross intrinsic value, before exercise costs and taxes. Ballve said that equity awards for administrative, support and entry-level roles are not uncommon at venture capital-backed companies. Historically, though, many companies phased out equity grants at hiring for these roles as they scaled up and salaries became more competitive, moving to performance- and tenure-based grants instead. After Anthropic goes public, the company will likely reserve upfront equity grants solely for recruiting top talent, he said.

Source: Reuters

Nov 18 : Millions of gamers around the world have logged on for the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," arguably the century's most anticipated video game, offering a glimpse of the vast, interconnected digital infrastructure the global economy increasingly relies on. No major disruption is expected from the rollout. But the scale of demand around one of the gaming industry's biggest releases underscores a broader risk for insurers: a failure at a shared cloud, payments or technology provider could affect thousands of businesses at once. After 13 years in development and an estimated $1 billion or more in production costs, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' began rolling out globally on Thursday, drawing the kind of attention that few entertainment releases ever command. But the fervour also underscores how much modern businesses depend on the digital infrastructure that makes such mass online activity possible, and the risks insurers face when that infrastructure fails.

"A launch of the scale of GTA VI is effectively a built-in stress test of the shared digital economy infrastructure," said Marcos Alvarez, managing director at Morningstar DBRS. Insurers cover businesses against financial losses stemming from disruptions to their operations, including some caused by technology failures. As companies increasingly rely on the same cloud providers, payment systems and digital platforms, a single outage could trigger claims from multiple policyholders at once, amplifying exposure. Despite the frenzy surrounding the launch, any disruption on launch day or in the days that follow would not necessarily spell disaster for insurers, industry experts said. "The recent technology outages have been a case in point with the gap between the economic cost and the actual insured loss being quite large due to policy limits, retentions, waiting periods, and coverage exclusions," Alvarez added. Business interruption could be a major source of claims, but coverage could also extend to costs associated with data recovery, system restoration, cyberattacks and outages at third-party technology providers, depending on the policy. "This is an area that is evolving rapidly for the insurance industry. Insurers are refining how they assess, model and manage these interconnected exposures," said Loretta Worters, a spokesperson for the Insurance Information Institute. "That means looking beyond an individual company's cybersecurity protections to understand its reliance on third-party providers, the concentration of those dependencies across their portfolios and the potential for a single event to generate losses across multiple policyholders."

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Texas has resumed issuing air permits for data centers, state regulators said on Wednesday, after pausing the practice last month as part of the state's broader attempt to manage the server warehouses and their effects on the electrical grid, communities and the environment. • The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality "has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations," TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said. • Texas Governor Greg Abbott halted the connection of new data centers to the state electric grid in August and ordered an audit of the projects, rattling one of the world's fastest-growing hubs for data center development. Abbott followed up by temporarily blocking air permits for all data center projects. • The air permit resumption came after the Texas grid operator notified the TCEQ that it had collected "community impact review" information for proposed data center projects, Lopez said.

The Abu Dhabi Global Market financial center serves as Binance's global hub, and the company said the Financial Services Regulatory Authority there is its primary regulator. Reuters was the first to report that Binance was granted a court order to aid asset recovery. Binance subsequently said in a blog post on Wednesday that, while it had absorbed the financial impact of the stolen funds and made customers whole, it had a responsibility to pursue the stolen assets and support law enforcement.  BILLIONS ALREADY FROZEN Binance has previously said that around $2.85 billion worth of the stolen crypto tokens had been frozen or intercepted by third parties. That includes Circle, which operates the stablecoin USDC, and World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture operated by US President Donald Trump's family, which has a stablecoin called USD1. Both tokens are pegged to the US dollar.  Under the court order, those firms and 16 others are required to maintain the freeze on the tokens involved in the heist, pending further court proceedings. They are also barred from lending, swapping or mixing the tokens with other assets.  El Salvador-based Tether, which issues the USDT token and previously said it had frozen $1.5 billion worth of the stolen funds, was not included in the court order. Bliss said Binance was working with Tether directly on the return of the frozen assets. "In consultation with the relevant authorities, we will work directly with Binance in respect of reissuing the tokens," a spokesperson for Tether said. Binance has hired US law firm Gibson Dunn as part of its efforts to recover the stolen crypto. In a statement, a lawyer from Gibson Dunn representing Binance called the injunction "one of, if not the, largest publicly known freezing orders ever made." FURTHER HEARING SCHEDULED A further hearing is scheduled for December 1, when the court will consider whether the proprietary injunction — a freezing order that applies to claimed assets — should continue and on what terms.  David Wachsman, spokesman for World Liberty Financial, said: "As the security incident unfolded in real time, World Liberty received an alert from onchain data identifying the issue. We acted decisively to protect our users and our partners." In a statement, a spokesperson for Circle said the company continues to coordinate with Binance and law enforcement, adding that Circle does not comment on specific legal proceedings.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Options on Anthropic shares could begin trading as soon as Monday, giving investors a new way to wager on the AI company's prospects as market participants expect heavy interest. Cboe Global Markets expects to list the contracts two business days after the stock begins trading, pending industry readiness. “The Anthropic IPO could be yet another catalyst, bringing a new wave of investors and trading activity to the options market," said Rob Hocking, Cboe’s global head of derivatives. "It’s great to see investor education driving this growth, as more people learn how options let them define their risk. An exciting trend and one we expect to continue.”  The Claude developer is expected to price its IPO later on Wednesday, and the shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday.   "We expect significant interest in Anthropic options once they list," said Garrett DeSimone, head quant at OptionMetrics. "The combination of AI-driven enthusiasm and the lottery-like payoff profile typical of IPOs are likely to draw investors immediately. As one of the most concentrated pure-play exposures to AI, the stock is also likely to be highly volatile."

Interest in Anthropic options could exceed the interest in SpaceX options earlier this year, said Ophir Gottlieb, chief executive of Capital Market Laboratories, citing oversubscription that is pushing the company's valuation higher and could invite various positioning ahead of the deal, as well as the market backdrop. "The AI trade is melting down," Gottlieb said. "Many feel it is overdone, while many others feel it's the popping of a bubble. Whenever there is such opposing views in a heated market, we get a lot of option positioning." Options give holders the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell shares at a set price within a certain period. They offer investors a cheaper way to gain exposure to a stock and to express their views on both short-term price moves and longer-term positioning. Anthropic’s $64 billion IPO has drawn stronger early institutional demand than the offering of SpaceX, with the book six times oversubscribed last week, Reuters previously reported. The IPO has drawn anticipation from investors, with Wall Street rolling out products tied to the stock, hosting client events and giving away merchandise ahead of the AI company's potentially record launch.

Nov 18 : While the causes of recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts and travel remain unclear, increased efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered vulnerabilities in the AI age are likely a major factor, according to cybersecurity experts and US officials. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters in Manila this week, said company patching efforts are, at times, "creating short-term disruption in the way the system works." Patches are software and operating system updates intended to fix security vulnerabilities found within a program or product. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing on worldwide threats Wednesday that there is so far no indication that the tech outages are related. But Clayton said the speed and level of capability of computer systems are "increasing substantially," so legacy computer systems and equipment that already were old are aging much more quickly.

The advent of easily accessible AI tools and large language models has supercharged the discovery of vulnerabilities in software. Microsoft this month has addressed more than 1,200 software vulnerabilities, nearly 20 times higher than in the same month a year ago, according to cybersecurity firm Qualys. At least one major bank was rushing to address a wave of recent patches and there is a lot of work needed, a source at the bank said, speaking on condition of anonymity.  "AI has made finding critical vulnerabilities fast and cheap, and the number of flaws that demand immediate patching has grown with it," said Yuval Itzchakov, CTO and co-founder of autonomous offensive security company A Security.  "Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle, and they are intrusive by design: they change runtimes, kernels and network components that everything else depends on. That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure," Itzchakov said. Josh Bressers, director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure at cybersecurity firm VulnCheck, said that in 2026 there have been 100,000 publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, tracked by industry as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVEs. Of those, Bressers said, 1,363 were known to have been exploited in the real world.  "Given tight resources for defenders, understanding which vulnerabilities need attention first is critical," Bressers wrote in a LinkedIn post. "Not all vulnerabilities are created equal." Anne Neuberger, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that AI is helping attackers find and weaponize vulnerabilities, but is a more "valuable friend" to those tasked with defending key computer networks. "AI is enabling enterprises to find 10 times more vulnerabilities," said Neuberger, who served as deputy national security adviser under former President Joe Biden and led incident response to serious national incidents. "And when patching at scale, some can cause problems." Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial, said technology has made banking "incredibly convenient, and while occasional outages can be frustrating I don't believe the outages will have a significant impact on consumer confidence or change how most people manage their money."  "Financial institutions have invested heavily in technology and security, and, unfortunately, occasional disruptions will happen," Gestiehr said. "What matters most is how quickly those issues are identified, resolved and communicated to customers."

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 18 : A gauge of stocks across the globe fell on Wednesday after Nvidia's quarterly results and ahead of Anthropic's market debut, while the dollar's strength on the back of a hawkish Federal Reserve weighed on trader sentiment. The dollar index strengthened to a fresh 19-month high after US Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC the central bank needs to either approve a half-point interest rate hike at its December meeting or communicate a faster pace of hikes in 2027. Mining stocks dragged European shares lower, while Nvidia's results initially helped Asian shares, with South Korea's Kospi up 2 per cent overnight. But the Nvidia rally fizzled and its stock fell 2.9 per cent after rising as much as 2.7 per cent. Nvidia's board dismissed the idea of rehiring former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week. The company's results and strong outlook did not dispel uncertainty.

"We believe (Tuesday's) results have stabilized sentiment and put a floor under the recent AI selloff, but they have postponed rather than permanently cured investor anxiety," said Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.11 per cent to 50,198.17, the S&P 500 lost 0.23 per cent to 7,323.63 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.42 per cent to 24,429.89.  MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe fell 0.45 per cent to 1,074.61. The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 1.03 per cent, while emerging market stocks fell 0.2 per cent. Japan's Nikkei rose 0.28 per cent to 59,024.28. The next health check on the AI industry will come as Anthropic prepares its market debut on Thursday. The company priced its initial public offering on Wednesday at $83 per share, above the expected range, according to a person familiar with the matter. DOLLAR UP, OIL DOWN In currencies, the dollar strengthened as Waller's comments and recent economic data cemented expectations for an interest rate hike next month. "The Federal Reserve seems at the moment to be very determined to hike interest rates and maybe even aggressively do so," said Juan Perez, senior director of trading at Monex USA in Washington. "That's the belief right now that's carrying the US dollar." The dollar index rose 0.17 per cent to 103.79, with the euro down 0.22 per cent at $1.0973. In commodities markets, crude prices fell after US crude and fuel inventories rose more than expected, adding to expectations of a supply surplus.  US crude lost 3.3 per cent to $83.17 a barrel and Brent fell to $91.84 per barrel, down 1.4 per cent. Spot gold dropped 3.24 per cent to $3,725.10 an ounce and spot silver fell 4.98 per cent to $45.04 an ounce. Copper declined 4.54 per cent to $12,626.00 a ton. Yields on 2-year US Treasury notes, which are sensitive to interest rate expectations, edged higher on hawkish Fed speaker comments and minutes from the last monetary policy committee meeting that underscored inflation worries. The 2-year note yield rose 1.31 basis points to 4.802 per cent, from 4.789 per cent late on Tuesday, while the benchmark US 10-year note yield fell 3.47 basis points to 5.068 per cent, from 5.103 per cent.
